summary: Describes the problem of rogue IPv6 Router Advertisements, where misconfigured or malicious devices announce themselves as routers and disrupt hosts that autoconfigure from those messages. It is a problem statement and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: An IPv6 Router Advertisement helps a host configure its network settings. If the host receives an unintended advertisement, it may use the wrong router or address prefix; RFC 6104 describes causes and possible mitigations.

questions: why are fake ipv6 router advertisements a problem
what is a rogue ipv6 router advertisement
how to stop rogue router advertisements
subtitle: Why unintended IPv6 Router Advertisements disrupt hosts and how operators can reduce the risk.

tldr.problem: IPv6 hosts use Router Advertisements to learn default-router and prefix information, so an unintended advertisement can give them incorrect network settings.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes administrator, user, and malicious sources of rogue advertisements and compares ten mitigation approaches, including switch filtering, SEND, host filters, and DHCPv6 options.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational problem statement focused mainly on accidental misconfiguration. The authors favor switch ACLs and RA-Guard-style approaches as practical options, while identifying SEND as a longer-term solution.

today: RFC 6104 is an Informational RFC published in February 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it discusses operational mitigations, including RA-Guard as specified by RFC 6105.

sections.title: What Makes a Router Advertisement Rogue
sections.content:
IPv6 hosts use Router Advertisements (RAs) to learn configuration information. The default router is taken from the source address of an RA, and the advertisement can provide prefixes used for stateless address autoconfiguration. A bogus or rogue RA is one that was not intended by the network's configuration.

Rogue RAs can cause partial or complete failure for hosts on a link. A host may select an incorrect default router or use a wrong prefix. The RFC focuses on accidental RAs because the authors considered them more common than malicious ones in the situations they describe.
sections.plainLanguage: A host uses router announcements to choose a default router and configure an address. An unintended announcement can give the host settings that do not work for the network.

sections.title: How Unintended Announcements Appear
sections.content:
The RFC groups rogue RAs into three broad sources. An administrator may configure a router or VLAN incorrectly. A user device may accidentally enable a service that sends RAs, or a user may connect cables in a way that bridges subnets.

An attacker may deliberately send RAs to cause denial of service or a man-in-the-middle attack. The document notes that its main focus is accidental misconfiguration; it does not attempt to analyze malicious RAs as part of a broader attack involving other Neighbor Discovery messages.
sections.plainLanguage: A wrong announcement can come from a network setup mistake, a user's device, or an attacker. The RFC concentrates on mistakes made by administrators or users.

sections.title: Mitigations and Their Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC surveys ten approaches. They include manual host configuration, RA snooping in switches, access-control lists on managed switches, Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND), router preference values, Layer 2 admission control, host packet filters, a tool that sends a deprecating RA, Layer 2 partitioning, and DHCPv6 gateway and prefix options.

Each approach has limits. Manual setup takes effort and can introduce mistakes; switch filtering requires managed equipment; admission control does not prevent a misconfigured authenticated user; and moving configuration to DHCPv6 creates a corresponding risk from rogue DHCPv6 servers. SEND can protect against rogue RAs in principle, but the RFC says deployment and implementation issues remained at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators can block suspicious announcements at switches, filter them on hosts, or use other network controls. Each method depends on equipment, configuration, or trust that may not be available in every network.

sections.title: Choosing a Response and Recovering
sections.content:
The RFC compares how the mitigations address administrator and user mistakes, then considers practical deployment. It says switch-based ACLs and RA-Guard-style approaches appear to be simple options where managed switches are available. Router preference and host firewalls may suit some managed environments, while SEND is described as a possible longer-term protection.

Detection and recovery matter too. Monitoring tools can report observed RAs, and administrators need a way to correct host configuration after a bad RA. The RFC also suggests isolating the source when possible. A deprecation tool must be used carefully, because sending a zero-lifetime advertisement for a genuine router could itself cause denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: No single mitigation fits every network. Operators need to detect incorrect advertisements, correct affected hosts, and avoid applying a protective action to the genuine router.

sections.title: Security Scope of the Document
sections.content:
The document focuses on operational problems caused by unintended misconfiguration. It says malicious RAs can look like accidental ones, although an attacker may spoof the genuine router's address or use a high router preference. The wider attack case, including malicious Neighbor Advertisements, is outside the document's scope.

Tools such as NDPMon may help administrators detect suspicious activity. The RFC also warns that a deprecation daemon could be abused to deprecate a genuine RA, so the mitigation itself needs protection.
sections.plainLanguage: A malicious announcement may resemble an accidental one. Monitoring can help, but a tool that sends corrective announcements must not be allowed to disable the real router.
